newsitem.title: UK: Defector blunts British Conservatives' optimism.
newsitem.headline: Defector blunts British Conservatives' optimism.

text.p: Optimism in Britain's ruling Conservative Party that its political prospects might finally be improving was blunted on Sunday by banner press headlines over the defection of a parliamentarian to the Liberal Democrats.

The decision by Peter Thurnham, who had been sitting in parliament as an independent Conservative, to join the minority party turned attention away from the Conservatives' new-found unity over Europe and back to allegations of corruption in the party.
"He (Thurnham) has put the cork very firmly back in the Tory champagne bottle," Peter Mandelson, a senior election strategist for the opposition Labour Party, told BBC television.

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, also speaking on BBC television, played down the importance of Thurnham's move, but said its timing seemed an attempt to cause maximum damage to Prime Minister John Major.

Major had taken heart from last week's annual conference of his party, which saw right-wing opponents bury the hatchet with him over a single European currency, an issue which has caused internecine warfare in the party for months.
They dropped demands that Major should rule out British membership immediately and accepted his call for the party to decide the issue after an election he must call by next May.

"Everyone in the Conservative Party should work -- and if I know them will work -- heart and soul, irrespective of personal interests, to secure re-election of a Conservative government," a relieved Major said in Friday's conference wind-up speech.
The Conservatives are at present 20 points behind Labour in opinion polls with the Liberals a distant third.

But Thurnham, who distanced himself from the Conservatives in February by refusing to accept parliamentary managers' voting instructions, said he was now leaving completely because the party had "lost touch with the basic values of decency".

Former minister Neil Hamilton is to be investigated by a parliamentary commissioner after admitting he accepted 10,000 pounds ($15,600) from a political lobbyist but denying claims he asked parliamentary questions for cash.
Critics say the commissioner lacks the powers to probe what they claim is widespread corruption among MPs, especially Conservatives.
"I cannot...accept the latest attempts by the government to suppress inquiries into allegations of sleaze, which poison the very basis of our democracy," Thurnham said in a statement.
Liberal leader Paddy Ashdown, who now has 26 MPs in the 651-member House of Commons, said Hamilton represented "the tip of the iceberg".
"I think -- I know -- that the sleaze issue is not one person, one incident, one time. It runs deep, it is systemic in the Conservative Party," he told Sky television.

Thurnham is the third Conservative legislator to leave the party in the past 13 months, and rumours swirled on Sunday that another could soon be on the way out -- this time a right-winger defecting to the tiny UK Independence Party.

Heseltine, asked by interviewer David Frost whether he could confidently predict there would be no more defectors, cautiously replied: "Well, I can't predict, David, that you will walk alive out of this studio."
